claim: Anthropic published a research post on provable inference on Nov 2, 2026, from its Frontier Red Team, with EPFL, MIT, StarkWare, RESI and Succinct co-authors.
quote: Roy Rinberg (Anthropic), Alex Allain (Anthropic); Alessandro Chiesa (EPFL, StarkWare), Miranda Christ (MIT, RESI), Rahul Dalal (Anthropic STEM Fellows Program, Succinct), Giacomo Fenzi (EPFL), Ben Mayer (Anthropic Fellows Program, MIT), Guy Weissenberg (EPFL)

claim: Anthropic says users today cannot verify that a response came from the claimed model rather than a substitute.
quote: A user querying a model today cannot check that the responses came from the specific model that a developer claims is responding, as opposed to one secretly substituted in by a routing service for cost reasons, or even by an attacker who has tampered with the token stream.

claim: Anthropic claims FlashProve proves Llama 4 Maverick (400B MoE) at about 110 tokens/s on one H100 with ~19 MB proofs, at ~70-95x vLLM GPU time.
quote: For a large model (Llama 4 Maverick, 400B-parameter mixture of experts), a single H100 GPU generates proofs at around 110 tokens/second, with a proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request, when in 4-bit quantized weights, using integer arithmetic in prefill. This is ~70-95x the GPU time of running the model itself on vLLM

claim: Anthropic reports verification takes 17 s on 24 threads (21 s single-thread) on a CPU, with a ~6.5 MB commitment download.
quote: The client downloads the commitment, ~6.5 MB in all, and then one proof per request. Checking a proof takes 17 seconds on 24 threads (and 21 seconds on a single thread), including the offline phase's checks.

claim: Anthropic reports the offline commitment takes about 39 minutes and lasts about 16 million requests; online proving of 24 requests takes about 223 s.
quote: The offline phase runs once per model and takes about 39 minutes. (For technical reasons we discuss in the technical report, the resulting commitment is good for about 16 million requests, after which the provider has to commit again.) The online phase, on a batch of 24 requests, takes the prover about 223 seconds, which is 110 tokens per second, and each proof is 18.78 MB.

claim: Anthropic says the commitment and proofs hide the weights but not the architecture.
quote: The commitment to the model, and subsequent inference proofs, hide the weights of the model; hiding the architecture of the model is not a goal of this system.

claim: Anthropic credits Claude with producing improvements to zkSNARKs for inference and writing the protocol specification.
quote: Claude has produced improvements on zkSNARKs for inference, building a system that is substantially faster than prior open-source systems.

claim: Anthropic frames the release as intermediate progress meant for others to build on.
quote: This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda. We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it.

claim: Anthropic says the prior proof of the same model (VerInf) took 14.3 hours for 1,000 tokens with a 93.6 GB proof.
quote: The only earlier proof of Llama 4 Maverick that we know of, VerInf, reports 14.3 hours for 1,000 tokens on a DGX Spark, with a 93.6 GB proof which took almost a day to verify.

claim: Anthropic states the fast C++ verifier carries no formal guarantee; only the slower Lean verifier is proved.
quote: Nevertheless, the C++ verifier is the one to use day to day: it carries no formal guarantee, and it agrees with the Lean verifier on every proof in our tests.

claim: Anthropic lists limitations: proofs cover an integer model under greedy decoding, and floating-point or sampled replies may diverge.
quote: A reply from a floating-point implementation, or sampled decoding, could depart at some position and no longer exactly match the computation proved.

claim: FlashProve currently handles only 1,024-token contexts.
quote: The system currently proves inference over contexts of up to 1,024 tokens. This is quite short in comparison to the contexts accumulated in chat settings.

claim: Side-channel attacks such as timing are out of scope.
quote: "side channel attacks", such as measuring the time it takes to produce a proof, could potentially reveal information about the weights. We consider this out of scope for this release.

claim: Anthropic says it met its provable-inference roadmap goal via a separate project that signs traffic and recomputes inference on a trusted server.
quote: As stated in our RSP updates, we met that goal through a separate but related project, which signs our inference traffic and recomputes inference on a trusted server; the work in this blog post pursues the same objective by a different method.

claim: Anthropic plans future work to hide architecture details.
quote: In future work we plan to also hide architecture details.

claim: The FlashProve repository is labeled an unmaintained research artifact under Apache 2.0.
quote: Version 0.16.0 · A research artifact: not maintained, not accepting contributions. · Apache 2.0

claim: FlashProve's own docs say a valid proof does not establish which real model the commitment is to; a provider could commit to a small or degenerate model.
quote: A yes does not say whose weights they are, that the shipped committer made the commitment, or which real model it is. A provider can commit to any model it likes, a small or degenerate one included

claim: In one repo measurement, the integer model's top token differed from the floating-point model at 6.81% of positions.
quote: in one measurement†, with a Python implementation of the integer model, the top token differed at 6.81 % of positions

claim: FlashProve's docs say weight hiding in the released programs is expected, not demonstrated.
quote: We expect, rather than know, that the programs hide the weights, within the bounds told under [Weight hiding](weight-hiding.md); few attacks were sought, and no test on the released programs hunts for a leak.

claim: Two published Fiat-Shamir attacks have not been examined against FlashProve.
quote: Two published attacks on Fiat–Shamir transformations (ePrint 2025/118; 2026/1838) have not been examined against this protocol or these programs.

claim: TechCrunch reports there are no plans to deploy FlashProve at Anthropic or any other lab.
quote: Research in the system is ongoing, and there are no plans to deploy it at Anthropic or any other lab.

claim: TechCrunch frames the system as guarding against model swapping, including by the lab itself.
quote: the researchers note that the system could be used to prevent an AI company from secretly swapping in a cheaper model to cut costs, or a more expensive model to inflate its performance results.

claim: Independent preprint (Hollow-LLM Attack) argues ZK inference proofs do not prove a provider actually ran a large model; 'ghost weights' can pass verification at small-model cost.
quote: These findings underscore that proof of correct inference is not proof of large-model execution and necessitate additional protections to bind correctness to verifiable computational work.

claim: Hollow-LLM describes the attack: keep the declared architecture and parameter count but embed ghost weights that collapse computation.
quote: a dishonest provider retains the declared architecture and parameter count but embeds ghost weights whose algebraic structure collapses effective computation

claim: RuntimeWire notes the overhead and token limit as reasons no provider has deployed such proofs.
quote: 70 to 95 times compute overhead and 1,024-token limit

claim: Hacker News reaction was minimal: two submissions of the post scored 9 and 6 points with zero comments.
quote: 50348831 9 0 2026-11-03T06:44:10Z Progress on provable inference for large language models; 50354148 6 0 2026-11-03T16:33:15Z Progress on provable inference for large language models
